newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Official sees changing role for EBRD in Hungary.
newsitem.headline: Official sees changing role for EBRD in Hungary.

text.p: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) sees its role in Hungary changing as the country has reached an advanced stage of its transition to market economy, Hubert Warsmann, head of the EBRD's Budapest office, said on Tuesday.
"We are constantly driven to do new things, and one of them is to get involved into private sector infrastructure," he told Reuters.
He added that EBRD's Hungarian portfolio represents some $1.5 billion and each dollar invested by the EBRD was followed by $2.5 from others.
But in a number of fields EBRD did only break the ice, as it was subsequently followed by others.

"A few years ago...you had to work very hard to convince other people to come along. Even in 1995, we brought five banks in a sindication for MOL. MOL has since done two or three transactions without us, without anyone," Warsmann said.

He added that the fact that Standard & Poor's gave Hungary's long-term foreign currency-denominated debt a triple-B minus rating on Monday would open the doors for investment that until now was not available to Hungary.
"For larger institutions that have very-very strict rules...the country was off-limits so far," he said.
Despite encouraging signs, Warsmann also sees some difficulties ahead for Hungary as well as other countries of the region in their transition to market economy.

"Most of the countries are only halfway down the road. There are still more reforms to tackle. Privatisation is not yet complete...they have to address the public sector reform, taxation reform and welfare reform," he said, declining to comment on the present stage of Hungary's welfare system reform.
As commercial banks broaden their areas of activity, the EBRD is gradually withdrawing from the centre of the market, he said.

"Commercial banks are a lot more active these days and we have a policy not to compete with them," Warsmann said, adding that since the beginning of the year there has been renewed interest by banks for Hungary.
He also said Hungary is unlikely to retain its privileged position in the region in attracting foreign direct investment as other countries are gradually picking up.
"What is the key, is to see that it grows in absolute terms and remains on the right track...but it would be vain to hope that Hungary's share of the total would remain constant," Warsmann said.
